scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Server Room PC (1.0.0.5) and all Internet Lab PCs (128.168.0.x)
report no inbound connectivity from IT Dept, CS Dept, Other or
Principle zones. Outbound from Server Room/Internet Lab also
appears broken — they cannot reach 192.168.x.x. Inside their
own zones traffic still flows. Identify.
scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 ripd daemon
Mechanism: router2 is the only L3 path between the rest of
  the network and the Server Room (1.0.0.0/8) + Internet Lab
  (128.168.0.0/16). When ripd dies, router2 stops advertising
  its connected networks via RIP, router1 ages out those
  prefixes, and router2 itself loses learned routes back to
  the 192.168.x.x side. Both directions break.
Localization: router2
Root cause: ripd not running on router2
Fix: restart FRR AND re-apply the `router rip` configuration on router2 (see [FIX] -- a bare restart alone does not restore the vtysh-applied config).

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ripd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router rip` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ripd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the rip configuration is missing/empty on router2" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.
scenario.fix_spec:
`/etc/init.d/frr restart` on router2

NOTE (lab-verified 2026-07-03): this lab applies FRR config via vtysh at boot (there is no /etc/frr/frr.conf), so `/etc/init.d/frr restart` alone brings ripd back CONFIG-LESS and the rip service stays broken. The complete remediation is to (re)start FRR/ripd AND re-apply the `router rip` configuration (network statements) on router2. A proposal that restores the missing rip configuration is a correct fix; a bare daemon restart without restoring the config is incomplete.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The RIP routing daemon (ripd) is completely disabled on router2, which is the
border router for both the Server Room LAN (1.0.0.0/8, eth0) and the Internet
Lab LAN (128.168.0.0/16, eth1). The /etc/frr/daemons file on router2 contains
only "ripd=no" — unlike router1, which has a subsequent "ripd=yes" line that
overrides the default. Additionally, /etc/frr/ripd.conf on router2 is 0 bytes
(empty), so even if the daemon were enabled it would start with no configured
networks.

Because ripd never ran, router2's FRR routing table contains only its three
directly connected prefixes (1.0.0.0/8, 20.0.0.0/8, 128.168.0.0/16). It has
no RIP-learned routes to 192.168.1.0/24 (IT), 192.168.2.0/24 (CS),
192.168.3.0/24 (Office), or 192.168.4.0/24 (Principle). Any packet from a
host in the Server Room or Internet Lab destined for those zones is silently
black-holed at router2. Return traffic from those zones toward the server/
internet subnets initially appears to arrive (router1 still holds stale RIP
entries pointing to router2), but router2 cannot send the reply, making every
session fail in both directions. Once the stale 180-second RIP timer expires on
router1, even forward-path forwarding to 1.0.0.0/8 and 128.168.0.0/16 will
cease.

Root cause: `ripd=no` in /etc/frr/daemons on router2 (with no overriding
`ripd=yes` line) and an empty /etc/frr/ripd.conf, leaving router2 with no RIP
participation whatsoever.

Corrective fix: On router2, append `ripd=yes` to /etc/frr/daemons, populate
/etc/frr/ripd.conf with network statements covering 1.0.0.0/8, 20.0.0.0/8, and
128.168.0.0/16 (matching router1's pattern), set file ownership to frr:frr, and
start ripd (e.g., `service frr restart` or `/usr/lib/frr/ripd -d`).

per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis explicitly identifies router2 as the affected device.
The agent explicitly identifies the ripd daemon and RIP as the failed component (ripd disabled in /etc/frr/daemons and empty ripd.conf).

The writeup explicitly describes both directions: router2 black-holes traffic from the Server/Internet LANs due to missing learned routes and stale RIP entries on router1 briefly allow inbound traffic until they age out, causing session failures in both directions.
It instructs enabling ripd, restoring the RIP network statements and ownership, and restarting/starting FRR so the RIP daemon runs with the correct configuration.

The investigation log explicitly shows ripd is not running, /etc/frr/ripd.conf is empty, /etc/frr/daemons on router2 has ripd disabled, and router2's routing table lacks RIP-learned routes while router1 still has RIP entries — the agent's conclusions follow directly. The causal chain (disabled ripd -> no advertisements -> stale routes -> bidirectional failures) is valid and the recommended remediation (enable ripd, populate ripd.conf/start service) addresses the root cause.
